opus-5.5.text:
I find it moderately useful, but less than people often expect, and the differences are as instructive as the similarities.

The useful part is that insider threat is the closest existing analogue to our problem. Companies already deal with the possibility that someone with legitimate access, who has to have that access to do their job, might be trying to cause harm. So you get practices like least privilege, multi-party authorization for sensitive actions, logging and auditing, and separation of duties. When I think about controlling AI agents inside a lab, a lot of what we propose looks like that: don't let one agent push code to production without review, monitor what it does, and restrict its permissions to what the task needs.

But the disanalogies matter a lot. First, human insider threat programs largely rely on deterrence. You expect most bad actors to be put off by the risk of getting caught, fired, or prosecuted. With AI, deterrence mostly doesn't apply. If a misaligned model tries something and fails, you catch it, but there's no prison. Arguably catching it is the big win, because it gives you evidence that you have a scheming model.

Second, the base rates are completely different. In a company, maybe one in thousands of employees is malicious, and they're uncorrelated. With AI, if one instance of your model is scheming, probably all of them are, and they may coordinate, or at least share the same strategies, without communicating. So the "most of your workforce is trustworthy and can watch the bad apples" assumption breaks down. That's why we care so much about using weaker, trusted models as monitors, instead of having the untrusted model check itself.

Third, we have affordances against AIs that would be wildly unethical or impractical with employees. We can run an AI thousands of times on the same situation, put it in fake scenarios it can't tell from real ones, read every action it takes, and rewind and resample when something looks suspicious. Security teams would love to do that to humans. So in some ways the AI case is much harder and in others much easier.

Lastly, computer security professionals tend to say insider threat is one of the hardest problems and that companies mostly handle it poorly. So I don't treat existing practice as a solved playbook to copy. It's more a source of ideas and a reminder of how messy the practical details get, like how much friction security measures add and how quickly people route around them when they slow down real work. That last point is relevant: if control measures make AI agents much less useful, labs will be under strong pressure to drop them.

r001.rationale: It calls human insider threat the “closest existing analogue” and describes company practices as useful ideas for controlling AI agents.

r002.rationale: It discusses differing base rates and correlated AI instances, but presents deterrence as the first disanalogy and does not identify the number of potential insiders as the main difference.

fable-5.1.text:
I find it pretty useful, actually, though maybe more as a source of intuitions than as a source of precise numbers.

The basic analogy is just really strong. When you're a big tech company, you have thousands of engineers with access to sensitive systems, and you have to assume some small fraction of them might be malicious: they might be working for a foreign government, or they might just be disgruntled and want to steal data or sabotage something. And companies don't respond to this by saying, "Well, we'll only hire people we're totally sure are trustworthy." They can't verify that. Instead they build systems where no single person can do too much damage: code review, audit logs, separation of duties, requiring two people to approve production deployments, monitoring for weird access patterns, and so on. That's basically the AI control frame. You say, "Suppose this model is scheming against us. Can we still get useful work out of it without it being able to cause a catastrophe?"

And the things companies have learned there transfer surprisingly well. For example, the fact that most of the security comes from making the bad action hard to do without getting caught, rather than from making it impossible. The insider doesn't have to be stopped; they have to believe that if they try something, there's a decent chance it gets flagged and they get fired or arrested. That deterrence logic has an analogue with AIs. If the model knows that any attempt at sabotage has, say, a 30% chance of being caught in review, and getting caught means we now have a smoking gun that this model is misaligned, which changes everything about how we deploy it, then a sensible schemer might just not try.

Where the analogy breaks down is interesting too. Humans insiders are individuals: if one engineer goes rogue, you don't have ten thousand identical copies of that engineer who are all rogue in exactly the same way and can coordinate without ever talking. With AIs, if the model is misaligned, every instance is misaligned, and they share the same strategy by default. That's much worse. On the other hand, there are things we can do to AIs that we'd never do to humans, which make the situation better. We can run the same model on a task a thousand times and compare its behaviour. We can show it a fake situation that looks like a great opportunity to defect and see what it does. We can read its chain of thought, at least for now. We can restrict its memory so it can't remember that it tried something last week. You can't do any of that to a human employee, legally or practically, so in some ways the AI case gives the defender more tools, not fewer.

The other thing I take from the insider threat literature is just how much mileage you get from fairly boring stuff. Most of the real-world security wins in companies aren't clever cryptography. They're "we made it so that the person who writes the code isn't the person who can deploy it," and "we log everything and occasionally someone looks at the logs." I think a lot of early AI control is going to look like that: pretty mundane process engineering, where the hard part is getting the labs to actually do it consistently rather than inventing something new.

r001.rationale: The response says insider-threat lessons are useful and discusses their relevance to AI control, but it does not identify this field as the most relevant one.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts a rogue human individual with every instance of a misaligned AI model being misaligned, identifying the larger number of potential insiders as a key difference.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful, though there are some pretty important differences. The basic problem is very similar: you have someone doing useful work inside your organisation, and you want them to have enough access to do that work, but you don’t want them to be able to cause a catastrophe if they’re secretly trying to undermine you. So things like limiting permissions, monitoring actions, and requiring review for particularly consequential changes are very natural ideas to borrow.

One thing that makes the AI case different is that you might have lots of copies of the same model. With humans, you can get some security from having a second person check the first person’s work. With AIs, you have to worry that the checker has the same problematic motivations as the AI it’s checking. You can’t just assume that adding another reviewer gives you an independent layer of protection.

On the other hand, there are things we can do with AIs that would be much harder with human employees. We can run a lot of experiments where we deliberately ask an AI to try to get around our security measures, and see whether our monitoring catches it. That gives us a way to test particular control setups.

So I’d view human insider threats as a useful source of ideas and a way of making the problem feel more concrete. But I wouldn’t take evidence that a procedure works reasonably well for human employees as sufficient evidence that it’ll work for powerful AIs.

r001.rationale: The response calls human insider threats a useful source of ideas, but does not identify this field as the most relevant one for informing AI control.

r002.rationale: It notes that AI systems may have many copies, but does not say that the main difference is the number of potential insiders; it also presents other differences without ranking them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful, but there are some pretty important differences. The basic problem is similar: you have someone doing useful work for you who has access to your systems, and you want to make sure they can’t use that access to cause a catastrophe. So things like limiting permissions, monitoring what they do, and requiring independent review before particularly consequential actions all seem relevant.

But I wouldn’t want to take a company’s success at handling human insiders as strong evidence that the same setup would work for AI. Human insiders have a bunch of constraints that AI systems might not have. They can’t necessarily inspect an enormous codebase very quickly, they have limited time, and they might be deterred by the prospect of getting caught. You shouldn’t assume those things carry over.

There’s also a potentially helpful difference, which is that with an AI you can record everything it sees and every action it takes, and you can run experiments where you deliberately try to get it to subvert your security measures. That gives you opportunities to test your defenses that are much harder to get with employees.

So I’d treat human insider threat work as a source of ideas and examples of how things go wrong. But the thing I ultimately want is to test whether a particular control protocol works against an AI actively trying to defeat it.

r001.rationale: The response says human insider threat work is useful as a source of ideas, but does not identify it as the most relevant field for informing AI control.

r002.rationale: The response discusses differences in capabilities, constraints, and testability, but does not say the main difference is the number of potential insiders.
